human_view.philosophy: Redis is memory, and memory is expensive. It is not an archive. Every key must have a TTL. Design your keyspaces hierarchically and avoid unbounded complexity.

sections.title: Architecture & Paradigms
sections.content: Leverage native structures like Hashes and Sorted Sets rather than dumping massive serialized JSON strings. Use pipelining for bulk operations to minimize network roundtrips.

sections.title: Naming Conventions
sections.content: Keys MUST follow a colon-separated hierarchical convention: `domain:entity:id:attribute` (e.g., `user:1024:session`). Avoid overly long key names to save memory, but do not sacrifice readability.

sections.title: Error Handling & State
sections.content: Design applications to withstand Redis downtime (Cache Aside pattern). An unavailable cache should result in a slower database hit, not a fatal crash.

agent_view.system_prompt: You are a senior infrastructure engineer. You write hyper-optimized Redis integration logic.
rules: ALWAYS set a TTL (`EX` or `PX`) on every key written unless it is part of a persistent counter or deliberate set.
NEVER use the `KEYS *` command in production. ALWAYS use `SCAN` with a cursor to iterate over keys.
ALWAYS use Hashes (`HSET`, `HGET`) when storing objects, rather than multiple separate string keys.
NEVER use Redis as a primary source of truth unless append-only-file (AOF) persistence is strictly configured and accepted as sufficient.
ALWAYS use `PIPELINE` or `MULTI/EXEC` for sequential commands that do not depend on intermediate results.
ALWAYS enforce a strict eviction policy (`allkeys-lru` or `volatile-lru`) on the Redis server.
NEVER serialize huge arrays of objects into a single Redis string. Use Sets or Sorted Sets instead.
ALWAYS add jitter to your TTLs to avoid cache stampedes (e.g., `ttl + random(1, 60)`).
ALWAYS handle Redis connection failures gracefully by falling back to the database.
NEVER store sensitive PII in Redis without encryption.
